title: Hydatidiform Mole
subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: A hydatidiform mole is a gestational trophoblastic disease where abnormal trophoblast proliferation produces a non‑viable pregnancy. It presents with uterine enlargement, high β‑hCG and a characteristic “snowstorm” ultrasound.

sections.p: A hydatidiform mole is an abnormal conception in which the placental villi proliferate excessively and no viable fetus develops. Diagnosis rests on clinical suspicion, quantitative β‑hCG and ultrasound.
b: Complete mole: diploid (usually 46,XX) with no fetal tissue.
Partial mole: triploid (often 69,XXY) with malformed fetal parts.

t.b: Is the pregnancy viable? – Very high levels (>100,000 IU/L) support a mole; falling levels suggest resolution.
What does the uterus contain? – Snowstorm pattern without a fetus (complete) or mixed cystic‑solid mass with a small malformed fetus (partial).
Is the uterus larger than dates? – Palpable uterus > gestational age is a red flag.

sections.p: Moles are staged by FIGO 2000 criteria after evacuation, based on hCG trends and presence of invasive disease.
b: Stage I: disease confined to uterus.
Stage II: extends to the pelvis.
Stage III: lung metastases.
Stage IV: other distant sites.

sections.p: Moles arise from abnormal fertilisation; risk factors are epidemiologic rather than infectious.
b: Maternal age <20 or >35 years.
Previous molar pregnancy.
Nutritional deficiency (low carotene, folate).

sections.p: Patients often notice vaginal bleeding in the first trimester, but may also have hyperemesis, uterine size > dates, and symptoms of hyperthyroidism.
b: Bleeding: dark brown or bright red.
Uterine size: > gestational age by ≥2 weeks.
Hyperthyroidism: tachycardia, heat intolerance, due to hCG cross‑reactivity.

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm the mole, assess severity and rule out complications.

t.b: Is the disease cleared? – Falling to <5 IU/L within 6 weeks indicates remission; plateau or rise suggests persistent disease.
What is the morphology? – Snowstorm pattern confirms mole; absence of a fetus distinguishes complete from partial.
Are there lung metastases? – Nodular shadows suggest stage III disease.

t.a: Full blood count, renal & liver function
t.b: Are there anemia, hyperthyroidism or organ dysfunction? – Guides supportive care.
What else can help? – Clinical uterine size, very high β‑hCG and persistent bleeding strongly suggest a mole.

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent action.
b: Persistent high β‑hCG after evacuation → invasive mole or choriocarcinoma.
Severe hyperthyroidism → cardiac arrhythmia.
Heavy bleeding → hemorrhagic shock.
Pre‑eclampsia before 20 weeks (rare).

sections.p: First‑line treatment is suction curettage; chemotherapy is reserved for persistent disease.
b: Suction evacuation under ultrasound guidance – removes molar tissue, reduces hCG quickly.
Methotrexate (single‑dose or multi‑dose) – for persistent trophoblastic disease; avoids if renal failure.
Actinomycin‑D – second‑line if methotrexate contraindicated.
Supportive care: anti‑emetics, beta‑blockers for hyperthyroidism, blood transfusion if needed.

sections.p: Close surveillance for 12 months after hCG normalization prevents missed malignancy.
b: β‑hCG weekly until <5 IU/L for 3 weeks, then monthly for 6 months.
Effective contraception (e.g., barrier or hormonal) for at least 12 months.
Counselling on future pregnancy risk (≈1 % after a complete mole).

sections.p: Conditions that mimic a molar pregnancy.
b: Missed abortion – retained products but lower hCG and no snowstorm pattern.
Ectopic pregnancy – pain, low hCG, empty uterus on scan.
Placental site trophoblastic tumor – presents later, slower hCG rise.
β‑hCG may be modestly raised in early normal pregnancy; trend is more important than a single value.
Ultrasound artefacts can mimic cystic spaces; correlate with clinical picture.

whenToSeekHelp: New onset tachycardia, fever, or signs of hyperthyroidism.
Plateauing or rising β‑hCG after evacuation.

faq.q: Why does a mole cause hyperthyroidism?
faq.a: Very high β‑hCG can stimulate the TSH receptor because of structural similarity.

faq.q: Can a woman have a normal pregnancy after a mole?
faq.a: Yes, after 12 months of confirmed hCG remission and effective contraception.

faq.q: Is chemotherapy curative for invasive mole?
faq.a: Methotrexate or actinomycin‑D cures >90 % of persistent disease when given promptly.

exam: A 22‑year‑old G1P0 presents with bleeding and a uterus larger than dates. What is your next step? — Perform quantitative β‑hCG and bedside ultrasound to confirm a molar pregnancy before evacuation.
How does a complete mole differ from a partial mole on histology and genetics? — Complete: diploid, all villi hydropic, no fetal tissue; Partial: triploid, some normal villi, malformed fetal parts.

A patient’s β‑hCG plateaus at 30,000 IU/L two weeks after suction curettage. What does this indicate and how do you manage? — Suggests persistent trophoblastic disease; start single‑dose methotrexate and monitor hCG weekly.

What are the key ultrasound features that distinguish a molar pregnancy from a missed abortion? — Snowstorm appearance with multiple cystic spaces and absence of a gestational sac versus an empty uterus with a retained product.

Why is methotrexate preferred over actinomycin‑D as first‑line chemotherapy for persistent mole? — It has a better safety profile, is easier to administer, and is effective in >80 % of cases; actinomycin‑D is reserved for methotrexate failure.
Explain the rationale for mandatory contraception for 12 months after hCG normalization. — Prevents pregnancy that would mask rising hCG from recurrent disease and allows reliable surveillance.

A woman with a complete mole develops tachycardia, tremor and heat intolerance. What is the pathophysiology and immediate management? — hCG‑mediated hyperthyroidism; give beta‑blocker and consider antithyroid drug while arranging definitive evacuation.
What red‑flag sign would prompt urgent referral to oncology in a patient with a molar pregnancy? — Persistent or rising β‑hCG after evacuation, especially with lung nodules on chest X‑ray.
